statement: In adults with moderate or severe PTSD who had stopped their psychiatric medicines (two phase 3 trials from one sponsor: 90 adults with severe PTSD in MAPP1, 104 with moderate to severe PTSD in MAPP2), MDMA given in three sessions within an intensive manualized therapy, compared with an inactive placebo given with the same therapy, reduced clinician-rated PTSD symptoms (CAPS-5, scale 0 to 80, baseline means about 44 and 39) at 18 weeks by 11.9 points more in MAPP1 (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) and 8.9 points more in MAPP2 (4.1 to 13.7); both arms improved substantially (in MAPP2, by 23.7 and 14.8 points). Among those assessed at 18 weeks, 67% vs 32% (MAPP1) and 71% vs 48% (MAPP2) no longer met PTSD criteria; counting everyone randomized, 61% vs 27% and 70% vs 39% (editors' calculation). Functional impairment improved slightly more with MDMA (SDS difference 1.2 points on a 0 to 10 scale in MAPP2). The two trials share their sponsor, design and therapy manual, and 18 of MAPP2's 19 named authors are also MAPP1 authors; most participants could tell their group and expectancy was not measured, so how much of the difference is due to MDMA itself is uncertain; no outcome after 18 weeks is reported, and no trial compares MDMA-assisted therapy with a trauma-focused psychotherapy. Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In two trials run for the same sponsor, adults with PTSD had three long therapy sessions with either MDMA or a dummy pill, plus the same talking therapy before and after. About 4 months later, PTSD scores had dropped more with MDMA: about 9 to 12 points more on a 0 to 80 scale. Of the people still checked, about 7 in 10 on MDMA no longer had PTSD, against 3 to 5 in 10 on the dummy pill. Most people could tell which pill they had, so part of the difference may come from what they expected. Nobody has reported what happened after 4 months, and MDMA has not been compared with standard PTSD talking therapy.
population: Adults with DSM-5 PTSD of at least 6 months, CAPS-5 of 35 or more (MAPP1) or 28 or more (MAPP2), after washout of psychiatric medicines; people with current substance use disorders (MAPP1) or most substance use disorders (MAPP2), personality disorders, cardiovascular disease or high suicide risk excluded
exposure: MDMA in three 8-hour sessions about a month apart, within a manualized therapy of three preparatory and nine integration sessions with a two-person team
comparator: Inactive placebo with the identical therapy
outcome: Change in CAPS-5 total severity from baseline to 18 weeks (primary); loss of PTSD diagnosis; SDS functional impairment
magnitude: MAPP1 (de jure MMRM, n = 89): difference 11.9 CAPS-5 points (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4), d 0.91 (0.44 to 1.37); registry least-squares means −24.5 vs −12.64. MAPP2 (n = 103): −23.7 (−26.94 to −20.44) vs −14.8 (−18.28 to −11.28); difference −8.9 (−13.70 to −4.12), d 0.7. Loss of diagnosis among those assessed: 28/42 (67%) vs 12/37 (32%) and 37/52 (71.2%) vs 20/42 (47.6%); with everyone randomized as denominator (editors' calculation): 60.9% vs 27.3% (difference 33.6 points, 14.3 to 52.9) and 69.8% vs 39.2% (30.6, 12.4 to 48.8). Remission 14/42 vs 2/37 and 24/52 vs 9/42. SDS: MAPP2 difference −1.20 (−2.26 to −0.14); MAPP1 P = 0.0116, d 0.43 (−0.01 to 0.88).

evidence.extracted: De jure MMRM (n = 89, 46 on MDMA): between-group difference in CAPS-5 change from baseline to 18 weeks 11.9 points (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4), P < 0.0001, d.f. 71; de facto estimand including off-treatment values (n = 90): P < 0.0001.

Completers' change −24.4 (SD 11.6; n = 42) on MDMA vs −13.9 (SD 11.5; n = 37) on placebo with the same therapy; d = 0.91 (95% CI 0.44 to 1.37) for the de jure and 0.97 (0.51 to 1.42) for the de facto estimand. Editors' calculation: the printed d equals the completers' raw difference of 10.5 points over their pooled SD of 11.55.

Loss of diagnosis at 18 weeks among completers 28 of 42 (67%) vs 12 of 37 (32%); remission 14 of 42 (33%) vs 2 of 37 (5%); Fig. 3 expresses these outcomes as percentages of all 46 and 44 randomized. Editors' calculation with those denominators: loss of diagnosis 60.9% vs 27.3% (difference 33.6 percentage points, 95% CI 14.3 to 52.9), remission 30.4% vs 4.5%.
Key secondary SDS: MMRM P = 0.0116, d = 0.43 (95% CI −0.01 to 0.88); completers' change −3.1 (2.6) vs −2.0 (2.4).

evidence.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03537014 › Study Record Dates; Outcome Measures; Results › Outcome Measures
evidence.extracted: Registered 14 May 2018 (posted 25 May 2018), before the first participant (21 November 2018), with change in CAPS-5 to 18 weeks as the primary outcome; registry least-squares mean change −24.5 (95% CI −28.28 to −20.71) on MDMA vs −12.64 (−16.61 to −8.66) on placebo (modified ITT, 46 and 44).

Eligible: DSM-5 PTSD for at least 6 months and CAPS-5 of 35 or more after washout of psychiatric medicines; excluded: current alcohol and substance use disorders, personality disorders, conditions making a sympathomimetic harmful. Baseline CAPS-5 44.1 (SD 6.04); comorbid major depression 82 of 90 (91.1%); 69 (76.7%) White.

The primary outcome was a short-term one, 2 months after the last experimental session; long-term follow-up data are to be published later; blinding of participants was not formally assessed and, the authors say, was challenging and possibly led to expectation effects.

De jure MMRM: least-squares mean change in CAPS-5 −23.7 (95% CI −26.94 to −20.44) on MDMA vs −14.8 (−18.28 to −11.28) on placebo with therapy; treatment difference −8.9 (−13.70 to −4.12), P < 0.001; d = 0.7; de facto −23.7 vs −14.8, P < 0.001.

At 18 weeks, among those assessed: response 45 of 52 (86.5%) vs 29 of 42 (69.0%); loss of diagnosis 37 of 52 (71.2%) vs 20 of 42 (47.6%); remission 24 of 52 (46.2%) vs 9 of 42 (21.4%). Editors' calculation with all 53 and 51 randomized as denominators: loss of diagnosis 69.8% vs 39.2% (difference 30.6 points, 95% CI 12.4 to 48.8).

evidence.locator: Fig. 1; Results › Demographics and baseline characteristics, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: 104 randomized (53 MDMA, 51 placebo); stopped treatment 1 (1.9%) on MDMA vs 8 (15.7%) on placebo; 52 and 42 in the de jure analysis at 18 weeks.

evidence.locator: Methods › Participants; Table 1; Results › Demographics and baseline characteristics, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Eligible: CAPS-5 of 28 or more, off psychiatric medicines; mean baseline CAPS-5 39.0 (6.6); 28 of 104 (26.9%) with moderate and 76 (73.1%) with severe PTSD; 35 (33.7%) other than White and 28 (26.9%) Hispanic or Latino.

The evaluations did not extend beyond 2 months after therapy; superiority over SSRIs cannot be assumed without a direct comparison; the notable effect in the placebo-with-therapy arm could suggest standalone value of the manualized therapy.
At study termination 49 of 52 (94.2%) on MDMA and 33 of 44 (75.0%) on placebo were certain or thought they had received the treatment they had in fact received.

Funded by MAPS and organized by MAPS PBC, which oversaw the collection, analysis and interpretation of the data; 18 of the 19 named authors are also authors of MAPP1 (editors' comparison of the two author lists).

evidence.locator: Results › Study and participant characteristics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 2); Table 1 (p. 3); Study limitations, 1st paragraph (p. 8)
evidence.extracted: A search of five databases, rerun in May 2025, found the two phase 3 trials and four smaller randomized trials, which used an inactive placebo (three trials) or low-dose MDMA (three trials) as comparator; all six reported conflicts of interest with MAPS.

grade.reasoning: Two randomized, prospectively registered phase 3 trials (194 analysed in the de facto sets), starting high. Risk of bias, one level: in both trials the outcome-measurement domain of RoB 2 is high, because the CAPS-5, although rated by blinded independent assessors, rests on what participants report, and most participants knew their group (94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo in MAPP2's end-of-study survey; not assessed in MAPP1); expectancy was not measured. A bias of this kind could plausibly account for part of a 9- to 12-point difference but is unlikely to account for all of it, given its size and consistency; rated against the possibility that it explains most of the difference (very serious), the certainty would be low (the strict reading). The de jure estimand drops off-treatment outcomes and placebo dropout was higher in MAPP2 (8 vs 1), but the de facto analyses agree and the likely bias from that dropout runs toward no difference. Inconsistency not rated down: both trials found differences in the same direction with overlapping intervals (d 0.91 and 0.7). Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to the trial populations, to the comparison with placebo plus the same therapy and to 18 weeks. Imprecision not rated down: both intervals exclude no difference, though their lower ends (4.1 and 6.3 points) are small relative to the 10-point change the FDA accepted as clinically meaningful for an individual. Publication bias not rated down: both registered phase 3 trials are published, but all randomized evidence comes from one sponsor, which is why the status is replicated by the same team rather than replicated.

statement: In the two phase 3 trials of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD, which compared MDMA with an inactive placebo, most participants could tell which group they were in: in MAPP2, at the end of the study 49 of 52 (94.2%) on MDMA and 33 of 44 (75.0%) on placebo correctly identified their group, most citing effects they felt or did not feel (Bang blinding index 0.92 and 0.55, editors' calculation; 1 means everyone right, 0 chance); MAPP1 did not assess blinding and reports only that at least 9 of 90 participants (10%) had guessed wrongly when told their allocation. The outcome assessors were independent and blinded to treatment and visit, but whether they could guess allocation was not reported, and the primary outcome, a clinician interview, rests on what participants report. Expectancy was not measured in either trial, and the MAPP2 authors' arguments that it was mitigated are indirect. The trials therefore cannot separate MDMA's pharmacological effect from participants' knowledge of their allocation and their expectations: how much of the 9- to 12-point difference reflects these is unknown. Certainty: low. Status: single study (MAPP2 is the only trial with a blinding survey).
plain: Both big MDMA trials used a dummy pill with no effects. In the second trial, people were asked at the end which pill they thought they had: 94 in 100 on MDMA and 75 in 100 on the dummy pill guessed right, mostly from what they felt. The first trial did not ask. The people who scored PTSD did not know who had what, but the scores came from what people told them, and nobody measured what people expected. So we cannot tell how much of the extra benefit came from MDMA itself.
population: Adults with moderate or severe PTSD in the two MAPS-sponsored phase 3 trials (MAPP1, 90; MAPP2, 104)
exposure: MDMA in three sessions with manualized therapy
comparator: Inactive placebo with the same therapy
outcome: Participants' identification of their allocation (blinding integrity); assessor blinding; measurement of expectancy
magnitude: MAPP2 end-of-study survey: correct 49/52 (94.2%) on MDMA and 33/44 (75.0%) on placebo; wrong 1/52 (1.9%) and 9/44 (20.5%); could not tell 2/52 (3.8%) and 2/44 (4.5%); Bang index (correct minus wrong over all respondents) 0.92 and 0.55 (editors' calculation). MAPP1: not assessed; at unblinding at least 7/44 (15.9%) on placebo and 2/46 (4.3%) on MDMA had believed they were in the other group (anecdotal). Expectancy: not measured in either trial.

evidence.extracted: End-of-study survey: on placebo 33 of 44 (75.0%) certain or thought they had received placebo, 9 (20.5%) thought MDMA, 2 (4.5%) could not tell; on MDMA 49 of 52 (94.2%) certain or thought MDMA, 1 (1.9%) thought placebo, 2 (3.8%) could not tell; reasons: positive mental or emotional effect 45 of 52 and positive physical effect 29 of 52 on MDMA, no effect 28 of 44 on placebo. Editors' Bang index: 0.92 and 0.55.

evidence.locator: Methods › Randomization and masking, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Outcomes rated by a central pool of independent assessors blinded to the design, visit, assignment, number of treatments and safety data, each doing one CAPS-5 per participant; participants asked to withhold their opinion on assignment; the blinding survey was given at study termination (visit 20). Assessors' guesses are not reported.

Treatment expectancy was not measured; the authors offer three observations as support for its mitigation: the groups did not separate after the first session, placebo dropouts did not all occur after the first session, and not all participants identified their treatment.
evidence.quote: several observations support expectancy mitigation in the current study

evidence.locator: Fig. 1; Fig. 3 (values printed on the bars); Discussion, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Five of the 8 placebo participants who stopped did so after the first session; after the first session Fig. 3 prints loss of diagnosis in 39.6% on MDMA vs 22.0% on placebo; the authors name disappointment from ineffective blinding as one possible reason for the placebo dropouts.
Lifetime MDMA use reported by 22 of 53 (41.5%) on MDMA and 26 of 51 (51.0%) on placebo; in the past 10 years by 13 (24.5%) and 18 (35.3%).

Blinding was not formally assessed; when told their allocation, at least 7 of 44 (15.9%) on placebo had believed they received MDMA and at least 2 of 46 (4.3%) on MDMA had believed they received placebo, which the authors call anecdotal; they say blinding of participants was challenging and possibly led to expectation effects, and that safety data collected by site therapists may have limited blinding.

evidence.locator: Methods › Randomization, masking and bias minimization, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: An inactive placebo was chosen with the FDA, the authors noting that low-dose MDMA had improved blinding in phase 2 but was less effective than inactive placebo; outcomes were rated by an observer-blind independent rater pool by video, and participants were told to withhold their opinion on assignment.
Lifetime MDMA use reported by 29 of 90 (32.2%), in the past 10 years by 19 (21.1%).

The review counts functional unblinding in four of six MAPS trials, with blinding maintained or partly maintained only in two trials that used low-dose MDMA as comparator; its Table 5 gives 95% correct guesses by participants in the 2011 pilot trial with an inactive placebo.
The trial's authors call blinding in psychedelic trials a tremendous challenge with no perfect solution and state that no flawless comparator exists for psychedelic-assisted therapy.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim about the trials' blinding (METHODS §6.3: descriptive claims start low). The figures come from one end-of-study survey in one trial (96 respondents of 104 randomized, 7 placebo participants missing), taken after participants had experienced their outcomes, which mixes recognition of drug effects with perceived benefit; MAPP1 offers only anecdote. None of this could plausibly reverse the finding that most participants identified their group, so no further downgrade. The consequence drawn (that the trials cannot separate MDMA's effect from expectancy and unblinding) follows from the design: an inactive placebo, a participant-reported outcome and no measure of expectancy. The size of any resulting bias is not estimable from these papers.

statement: In the two phase 3 trials of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD (99 people given MDMA and 95 given an inactive placebo, with the same therapy, during about 3 to 4 months of treatment), MDMA compared with placebo increased common, mostly mild or moderate, short-lived adverse events: muscle tightness in 58.5% vs 25.5% (MAPP2) and 61% vs 14% (MAPP1, registry), and more often decreased appetite, nausea, hyperhidrosis, feeling cold, restlessness, mydriasis, bruxism and nystagmus, with transient rises in blood pressure and pulse during sessions. Serious adverse events were rare and occurred only on placebo (2 of 44 in MAPP1, none in MAPP2); severe events occurred in 5 of 53 vs 2 of 51 and mild cardiac events, mostly palpitations, in 7 vs 1 (MAPP2). Suicidal ideation was common in both arms and never rose above baseline; active ideation with some intent emerged in 2 MDMA and 1 placebo participant in MAPP2. No events were coded as misuse or abuse potential. How events were recorded limits these figures: expected effects such as euphoria were deliberately not recorded as adverse events (MAPP1); events were collected by site staff (therapists, in MAPP1), who were probably aware of allocation; relatedness was not assessed except for serious events (MAPP2); attribution to MDMA rested on a twofold difference in frequency; the MAPP1 registry lists substance-use events in 3 vs 0 participants, which the article does not mention; and the trials excluded cardiovascular disease, most substance use disorders and high suicide risk and ended at 18 weeks, too few people and too short to show rare or delayed harms such as later misuse. Certainty: moderate (for the increase in common adverse events). Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In two trials, 99 people took MDMA and 95 took a dummy pill, in a clinic, with therapy. MDMA often caused short-lived side effects: tight muscles (about 59 to 61 in 100 people, against 14 to 26 in 100 on the dummy pill), less appetite, sickness, sweating and feeling cold, and blood pressure and pulse went up for a while during sessions. No serious side effects were seen on MDMA; two people on the dummy pill had one. Thoughts of suicide were common in both groups and did not go up. But the trials did not record some expected effects, like feeling very happy, and were too small and short to show rare harms or misuse later on.
population: Adults with moderate or severe PTSD in the two MAPS-sponsored phase 3 trials (MAPP1, 90; MAPP2, 104), excluding cardiovascular disease, most substance use disorders and high suicide risk
exposure: MDMA in three supervised 8-hour sessions with manualized therapy
comparator: Inactive placebo with the same therapy
outcome: Treatment-emergent adverse events from the first experimental session to the last integration session (common, severe, serious, cardiac, suicidality and misuse-related events), as recorded
magnitude: MAPP2 (53 vs 51): muscle tightness 58.5% vs 25.5% (editors' difference 33.0 points, 95% CI 15.1 to 50.9); nausea 45.3% vs 21.6%; decreased appetite 35.8% vs 9.8%; hyperhidrosis 34.0% vs 5.9%; severe events 9.4% vs 3.9%; serious 0 vs 0; cardiac 7 vs 1; psychiatric 83.0% vs 72.5%; events of special interest 11.3% vs 5.9%. MAPP1 (46 vs 44; registry counts over about 18 weeks): muscle tightness 28 vs 6 (editors' difference 47.2 points, 29.9 to 64.6); decreased appetite 24 vs 5; nausea 14 vs 5; hyperhidrosis 10 vs 1; serious events 0 vs 2; suicidality events of special interest 3 (6.5%) vs 5 (11.4%); abuse-potential events 0 vs 0; substance use 3 vs 0.

evidence.extracted: Treatment-emergent adverse events more frequent on MDMA were typically transient and mild to moderate: muscle tightness, decreased appetite, nausea, hyperhidrosis and feeling cold; transient rises in blood pressure and heart rate on MDMA; a temperature of 38.1 °C in two MDMA participants.

Adverse events at 5% or more (first experimental session to termination visit, about 18 weeks; 46 vs 44): muscle tightness 28 vs 6, decreased appetite 24 vs 5, nausea 14 vs 5, hyperhidrosis 10 vs 1, feeling cold 9 vs 3, mydriasis 7 vs 0, restlessness 7 vs 0, nystagmus 6 vs 0, bruxism 6 vs 1, blood pressure increased 5 vs 0; suicidal ideation 21 vs 21; serious events 0 vs 2.

Serious adverse events: three in two placebo participants (suicidal behaviour; suicidal ideation leading to self-hospitalization), none on MDMA; suicidality events of special interest 3 (6.5%) on MDMA vs 5 (11.4%) on placebo; cardiac events that could indicate QT prolongation 0 vs 1; abuse potential 0 vs 0.

Suicidal ideation at baseline in 17 of 46 (37%) on MDMA and 14 of 44 (32%) on placebo; during the study the number with ideation never exceeded baseline, and serious ideation (C-SSRS 4 or 5) occurred almost entirely on placebo.
Expected effects of MDMA, such as euphoria, stimulation and feelings of closeness, were not solicited as adverse events, to avoid biasing adverse-event collection.
evidence.quote: intentionally not solicited as adverse events

evidence.locator: Methods › Statistics and reproducibility, 10th paragraph; Discussion, 10th paragraph
evidence.extracted: An association with MDMA was inferred from at least a twofold difference in incidence between arms; safety data were collected by site therapists, which the authors say may have limited the blinding of those data.

Abuse potential was monitored by coding adverse-event terms for dependence, intentional product misuse, overdose or diversion as events of special interest; the drug was given only in supervised sessions in a controlled clinical environment.

evidence.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03537014 › Results › Adverse Events (other adverse events)
evidence.extracted: Substance use (social circumstances) recorded in 3 of 46 on MDMA and 0 of 44 on placebo; no term for euphoria is listed; the article does not mention substance-use events.

At least one adverse event 53 of 53 vs 49 of 51; severe 5 (9.4%) vs 2 (3.9%); serious 0 vs 0; leading to discontinuation 0 vs 2; events of special interest 6 (11.3%) vs 3 (5.9%), none for misuse, physical dependence or diversion. Muscle tightness 31 (58.5%) vs 13 (25.5%); nausea 24 (45.3%) vs 11 (21.6%); decreased appetite 19 (35.8%) vs 5 (9.8%); hyperhidrosis 18 (34.0%) vs 3 (5.9%).

Cardiac adverse events in 7 on MDMA vs 1 on placebo, all mild (palpitations 5 vs 1; tachycardia 2 vs 0); vascular events 7 vs 2, all mild except one moderate hypertension; temporary dose-dependent rises in blood pressure and pulse during sessions, needing no intervention.

Psychiatric adverse events 44 (83.0%) vs 37 (72.5%); severe psychiatric events 3 vs 2; suicidality events of special interest 2 vs 2; active ideation with some intent (C-SSRS 4 or 5) in 2 MDMA and 1 placebo participant on 5 occasions; the number with ideation never exceeded baseline in either arm.

evidence.locator: Methods › Outcomes, 3rd paragraph; Statistical analysis, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Adverse events counted from the first experimental session to the last integration session, severity graded by the site physician; except for serious events, relatedness to the drug was not assessed, to preserve blinding; events were attributed to MDMA when more than 10% and at least twice as frequent as on placebo.

Participants with any substance use disorder other than cannabis or alcohol in the previous 12 months, or with severe or moderate (early remission) alcohol or cannabis use disorder, were excluded, as were people at high suicide risk or with personality disorders or cardiovascular disease; the authors say long-term data are needed on misuse after the trial.

evidence.locator: Safety of MDMA-AT: adverse events, 1st paragraph (p. 4); Discussion, 1st paragraph starting on p. 9
evidence.extracted: Adverse-event reporting varied substantially between trials, depending in part on the measure used, and documentation in the literature was inconsistent, making synthesis difficult.
Rare adverse events are difficult to evaluate in phase 3 trials with limited samples and no long-term follow-up, and can become noticeable only when a treatment is widely used.

grade.reasoning: Two randomized trials, starting high. Risk of bias, one level: adverse events were collected by site therapists who were probably aware of allocation, expected drug effects were deliberately not recorded (MAPP1), relatedness was not assessed and attribution rested on a twofold difference; these affect what was counted, though they could not plausibly create differences as large as those in muscle tightness, appetite, nausea and sweating. Inconsistency not rated down: the same events dominate both trials. Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to the treatment period and the trial populations. Imprecision not rated down for the common events, whose intervals are far from no difference; serious, severe and cardiac events, suicidality and misuse are too few to compare, and the claim says so rather than claiming no increase (METHODS §6.3). Both trials are from one sponsor, hence replicated by the same team.

statement: Whether the phase 3 trials show that MDMA itself, given within an intensive therapy, is an effective and acceptably safe treatment for PTSD is contested, and the papers read here cannot settle it. Two randomized trials from one sponsor (MAPP1, 90 adults; MAPP2, 104) found larger falls in PTSD symptoms with MDMA than with placebo plus the same therapy at 18 weeks (11.9 and 8.9 CAPS-5 points; see the claim on the trials' efficacy in section 12) and no serious adverse events on MDMA during treatment. Against this, most participants could tell their group while expectancy went unmeasured; the comparator was placebo, not a trauma-focused psychotherapy; no outcome after 18 weeks is reported; expected drug effects were not recorded as adverse events; and the trials' design and background claims rest partly on pooled phase 2 analyses that were retracted in 2024, as a 2025 review reports. Certainty: low. Status: contested.
plain: Is MDMA, given with talking therapy, a good and safe treatment for PTSD? Not settled yet. Two trials run for the same sponsor found that PTSD eased more with MDMA than with a dummy pill and the same therapy, over about 4 months, with no serious side effects on MDMA. But most people could tell which pill they had, nobody measured what they expected, MDMA was not compared with standard PTSD talking therapy, nobody has reported what happened later, and some earlier results used to plan the trials were withdrawn in 2024.
population: Adults with PTSD considered for MDMA-assisted therapy
exposure: MDMA in three sessions within a manualized therapy
comparator: The same therapy with placebo; trauma-focused psychotherapy; the course of PTSD after treatment ends
outcome: PTSD symptoms beyond the trial period and harms in clinical use attributable to MDMA itself
magnitude: Not estimable as an effect of MDMA separate from expectancy, or beyond 18 weeks. The trials' between-group differences at 18 weeks are 11.9 (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) and 8.9 (4.1 to 13.7) CAPS-5 points; 94% and 75% of MAPP2 participants identified their allocation.

evidence.extracted: MAPP1: CAPS-5 difference 11.9 points (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) at 18 weeks in favour of MDMA (n = 89), P < 0.0001.
MAPP2: CAPS-5 difference −8.9 points (95% CI −13.70 to −4.12) at 18 weeks in favour of MDMA, P < 0.001; placebo with therapy improved by 14.8 points.

evidence.locator: Results › Exploratory outcomes, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 8th paragraph
evidence.extracted: At study end 49 of 52 (94.2%) on MDMA and 33 of 44 (75.0%) on placebo identified their allocation; treatment expectancy was not measured.

Blinding was not formally assessed; the authors say blinding of participants was challenging and possibly led to expectation effects, and that the result is a short-term outcome 2 months after the last session, with long-term data to follow.
The evaluations did not extend beyond 2 months after therapy; long-term effectiveness depends on an ongoing follow-up (NCT05066282).
Expected effects of MDMA such as euphoria were not solicited as adverse events, and safety data were collected by site therapists.

evidence.locator: Methods › Randomization, masking and bias minimization, 2nd paragraph; References 15
evidence.extracted: The choice of an inactive placebo is justified by citing the pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials (reference 15, Mithoefer et al., 2019).

evidence.locator: Results › Study and participant characteristics, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: In August 2024 the pooled phase 2 analyses by Mithoefer et al. (2019) and Jerome et al. (2020) were retracted because both included data from a site where a serious ethical violation occurred.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph starting on p. 9 (right column)
evidence.extracted: As described without a citation: an FDA advisory panel voted against recommending MDMA-AT, concluding that efficacy was not sufficiently shown and benefits did not outweigh risks, with concerns including potential functional unblinding, unstandardized psychotherapy across sites, suicidal ideation, cardiovascular risk and potential misuse.

evidence.locator: Efficacy of MDMA-AT for PTSD, 1st paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Five of the six MAPS-linked randomized trials found a significantly greater CAPS decrease with MDMA; the sixth found a non-significant decrease against low-dose MDMA.

The critics argue that a breakthrough claim requires comparison with first-line trauma-focused psychotherapies, which on cross-trial figures reach similar symptom reductions with half or less of MAPP1's therapist time (the equivalent of 28 sessions of 90 minutes with two therapists).

The trial's authors reply that comparison with psychological interventions is not part of a regulated phase 3 drug programme, that both arms received the same psychotherapy to isolate MDMA's contribution, and that no flawless comparator exists.
Both trials were funded by MAPS and run by MAPS PBC; 18 of MAPP2's 19 named authors are also MAPP1 authors (editors' comparison of the author lists).

grade.reasoning: Rated for the question as posed, which goes beyond what the trials measured. Starting high (randomized trials). Risk of bias, one level, as in the efficacy claim: unblinding with a participant-reported outcome and unmeasured expectancy. Indirectness, one level: the question concerns MDMA's own contribution, durability beyond 18 weeks, comparison with existing psychotherapy and harms in clinical use, none of which the trials measured directly. The short-term comparison with placebo plus the same therapy is rated separately (moderate, section 12). Contested (METHODS §6.4): credible published critiques and the 2024 regulatory events change the interpretation of the trials.

debate.question: Do the phase 3 trials show that MDMA, given with therapy, is an effective and acceptably safe treatment for PTSD?
debate.evidence_yes: Two prospectively registered, randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials with central randomization and blinded independent assessors found larger falls in clinician-rated PTSD symptoms with MDMA than with placebo plus identical therapy at 18 weeks: 11.9 points (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) in 90 adults with severe PTSD and 8.9 points (4.1 to 13.7) in 104 adults with moderate to severe PTSD; 67% vs 32% and 71% vs 48% of those assessed no longer met PTSD criteria (61% vs 27% and 70% vs 39% of everyone randomized, editors' calculation) (Mitchell et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2023). The registered primary outcomes are those reported, and analyses that included off-treatment data agreed. The benefit was seen in people with long-standing PTSD, high rates of depression and the dissociative subtype, and again in a more diverse second sample, where only 1 of 53 people stopped treatment on MDMA against 8 of 51 on placebo. No serious adverse event occurred among the 99 people given MDMA; common effects were short-lived and mostly mild; suicidal ideation never rose above baseline in either arm; no events were coded as misuse (Mitchell et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2023). The trial's authors argue that phase 3 drug trials are designed to isolate the drug against placebo with the same therapy and that no flawless comparator exists (Mitchell, Coker & Yazar-Klosinski, 2021). A systematic review counted five of six MAPS-linked randomized trials as finding significant benefit (Brett & Bynum, 2025).
debate.evidence_no: Most participants knew their group: in MAPP2, 94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo identified it at the end of the study, mostly from the effects they felt or did not feel; MAPP1 did not assess blinding; neither trial measured expectancy; and the outcome, although rated by blinded assessors, rests on participants' reports (Mitchell et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2023). The MAPP2 authors' arguments that expectancy was mitigated are indirect: five of the eight placebo participants who stopped did so after the first session. Both trials were funded by one sponsor, which designed, analysed and helped write them, and 18 of MAPP2's 19 named authors are also MAPP1 authors (editors' comparison); the review found no randomized trial without a link to MAPS (Brett & Bynum, 2025). The comparator was placebo, not a trauma-focused psychotherapy, and the placebo-with-therapy arm also improved substantially (by 14.8 points in MAPP2); critics argue that a breakthrough claim needs benchmarking against first-line psychotherapies, which on cross-trial figures reach similar effects with half or less of the therapist time (Halvorsen, Naudet & Cristea, 2021). No outcome after 18 weeks is reported. Expected effects such as euphoria were not recorded as adverse events, events were collected by site therapists, and the trials excluded people with cardiovascular disease, most substance use disorders and high suicide risk; the MAPP1 registry lists substance-use events in 3 of 46 participants on MDMA and none on placebo (Mitchell et al., 2021). The pooled phase 2 analyses cited for the choice of an inactive placebo and for durability were retracted in 2024 because they included data from a site with a serious ethical violation, and an FDA advisory panel voted against the treatment, citing among other concerns potential functional unblinding (both as reported by Brett & Bynum, 2025).
debate.neither_can_show: With an inactive placebo, neither the trials nor their critics can separate MDMA's pharmacological effect from participants' knowledge of their allocation and their expectations, and no trial measured expectancy or the assessors' guesses. Two trials of under 200 people followed for 18 weeks cannot show rare harms, later misuse or durability. No trial compared MDMA-assisted therapy with a first-line psychotherapy, so the cross-trial comparisons of effect sizes and remission rates made by both sides rest on different control conditions and populations.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: low). In two trials from one sponsor, MDMA within an intensive therapy led to larger short-term falls in PTSD symptoms than placebo with the same therapy, without serious adverse events on MDMA during treatment (moderate certainty for that comparison; see the efficacy and adverse-event claims in section 12). How much of the difference is due to MDMA rather than to unblinded expectation, whether it lasts beyond 18 weeks, how it compares with trauma-focused psychotherapy and what harms appear in wider use are not answered by the papers read here. Missing from this reading: the regulator's own briefing documents and decision, the retraction notices, the second critique of MAPP1 (Burke & Blumberger, 2021), the trials' supplementary tables and the phase 3 long-term follow-up.
debate.what_would_settle_it: An independent, preregistered trial with an active comparator that mimics MDMA's noticeable effects (or several doses), expectancy measured before treatment and blinding during it, assessors' guesses recorded, adverse events collected by staff outside the therapy team, and follow-up of at least 12 months; a trial against a trauma-focused psychotherapy of matched therapist time; publication of the phase 3 long-term follow-up for both arms; and the regulator's briefing documents and review.
